image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #827: My Business Idea

titleText.es: Al principio no te creíamos, pero le preguntamos a unas tres personas que estuvieron en esa fiesta. No solo corroboraron tu historia, sino que además dijeron que mencionaste que querías montar una empresa algún día. ¡Lo sentimos! Si esto no es suficiente dinero, dínoslo.
titleText.en: We didn't believe you at first, but we asked like three people who were at that party. They not only corroborated your story, but even said you totally mentioned wanting to start a company someday. Sorry! If this isn't enough money, let us know.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd. OCR omitted most small form text and the right-hand button and delivery panel, split SOLICITAN-/DO, lost several accents and initial letters, and fused several form labels. The monetary amount, percentages, address, English button label, personal name, and delivery-company logo are audited exclusions. Cursor art, form borders, browser controls, hand pointer, dollar markings, figures, furniture, and speech tails are structural artwork.

regions.labelEs: ¡TÍO! ¡TUVE ESTA IDEA HACE COMO CINCO AÑOS, Y UNA EMPRESA SE HA HECHO RICA CON ELLA!

applications.explanationEn: Hace places the idea in the past, como makes the quantity approximate, and cinco años gives the duration.
Ha is the present helper for a singular company, and hecho is the irregular participle of hacer.
Se and hecho form hacerse, ha places the change in the present perfect, and rica names the resulting state.
Rica uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun empresa.

regions.labelEs: CLARO QUE SÍ. ESTOY SOLICITANDO MI PARTE AHORA.

applications.explanationEn: The fixed three-word expression gives a confident positive answer.
Estoy is the first-person present helper, and solicitando presents the formal request as ongoing.
Espera is the affirmative tú command used to tell one familiar listener to wait.
Qué is a direct question word and therefore keeps its written accent.

regions.labelEs: FECHA EN LA QUE TUVISTE LA IDEA: HACE COMO CINCO AÑOS.

applications.explanationEn: En supplies the time relation, la agrees with the feminine antecedent fecha, and que introduces its description.
Tuviste presents having the idea as a completed event at the requested past date.
Hace places the event in the past, como makes the quantity approximate, and cinco años gives the duration.

regions.labelEs: PRUEBA DE QUE LA TUVISTE: SE LO DIJE A MI AMIGO MIKE. ¡PUEDES PREGUNTARLE! YO ESTABA EN PLAN «¿SABES LO QUE SERÍA UNA BUENA IDEA PARA UN NEGOCIO?» Y ÉL RESPONDIÓ

excludedUnits.rationale: This personal name is excluded while all surrounding Spanish form text is taught.

applications.explanationEn: Prueba names the evidence, de que introduces its content, and la tuviste supplies the complete claim being supported.
Se comes before lo: se refers to the person told, while lo stands for the thing that was said.

applications.exampleEs: SE LO DIJE A MI AMIGO
applications.explanationEn: The later phrase a mi amigo makes the person represented by se explicit; se is required instead of le before lo.
Puedes is the form of poder for one familiar listener, and preguntar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside preguntarle, with le attached.
Le attaches to the end of the unchanged infinitive preguntar to identify one person being asked.
Estaba already identifies a first-person subject, so printed yo adds explicit focus before the quoted recollection.
Estaba sets a past state, and en plan colloquially frames the loose quotation that follows.
Neutral lo and relative que combine to refer to an unspecified idea or thing.
The ordinary statement-shaped frame sabes lo que sería remains in place; the surrounding question marks and intonation make it a yes-or-no question without an extra helper word.
Sería supplies the ‘would be’ form of ser for the imagined good idea.
Buena appears before idea because it gives an evaluation of the idea as a whole.
Buena uses feminine singular -a to agree with feminine singular idea.
Tuviste presents having the idea as a completed past event.
Dije presents telling the friend as a completed past event.
Estaba supplies an ongoing background state before the remembered quotation.
Respondió presents the reply as a completed past event.

applications.explanationEn: Parte is the thing deserved, while te comes before mereces, the form used for one familiar person in the present.
Que links parte to the description te mereces, which identifies the particular share.
Sé is the irregular affirmative tú command of ser and keeps its written accent.

applications.explanationEn: Dirección names the address, and postal specifies that it is used for mail.
Postal follows dirección because it classifies the kind of address.
Postal is singular to agree with singular dirección; its ending does not change for feminine gender.

cards.noteEn: Tío literally means “uncle,” but in casual speech in Spain it can address a male friend much like “dude” or “man.”

example.es: Tío, no me lo puedo creer.

cards.noteEn: Tuve is the completed-past form of tener for the speaker. This completed-event past is called the preterite.
Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.

cards.promptEs: idea antigua · empresa rica · solicitar una parte · formulario retroactivo
cards.questionEn: Why does the business-idea department turn the speaker's complaint into a joke?
cards.answerEn: It treats a vague old remark as if it were formal evidence that entitles someone to a retroactive share of a company's profits.
cards.noteEn: The speaker first makes the familiar claim that a company got rich from an idea he had years earlier. The next panels imagine an official form accepting hearsay, an approximate date, a self-selected percentage, and a mailing address, followed by an implausibly immediate cash delivery.
Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.
Before a number or amount of time, como can show that the amount is approximate rather than exact.
Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.noteEn: Empresa is a feminine noun for a company or business organization.

example.es: La empresa abrió una oficina pequeña.
example.en: The company opened a small office.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps hacerse mean ‘to become’
cards.noteEn: With a describing word, hacerse can present a gradual or noticeable change in the subject's state.

example.es: Los días se hacen más largos.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that a person or thing becomes or gradually grows a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by the word that describes the new state.
cards.noteEn: The short marker and hacer form change with the subject: me hago, te haces, se hace, nos hacemos, and so on. The describing word matches the person or thing in number and, when its form changes, gender.

example.es: Las tardes se hacen más cortas.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer. With se and a form of haber, it helps form hacerse + description, meaning to become or grow into a new state. After haber, hecho does not change to match a feminine or plural subject.

example.es: El barrio se ha hecho famoso.

cards.noteEn: Rica matches the feminine singular noun gente even though gente refers to multiple people.

example.es: La gente rica vivía en ese barrio.
example.en: Rich people lived in that neighborhood.

cards.answerEn: it (referring to a feminine thing after a preposition)
cards.noteEn: After a preposition such as en, con, or de, ella can refer back to a feminine singular thing as well as to a woman. English normally uses “it” for the thing.

example.es: La caja está vacía; no hay nada en ella.
example.en: The box is empty; there is nothing in it.

cards.noteEn: Parte can mean one portion of a whole. In money or ownership contexts, it can be the share that belongs to a person.

example.es: Cada socio recibió su parte de las ganancias.
example.en: Each partner received their share of the profits.

cards.questionEn: How can you give a confident 'of course' answer to a yes-or-no question?
cards.noteEn: Claro que sí strongly confirms a positive answer. Claro que no gives the corresponding confident negative answer.

cards.answerEn: that (fixed linker in claro que sí)
cards.noteEn: In claro que sí, que links claro to the emphatic sí. Learn the three words together as a common expression of confident agreement.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Solicitando is the -ando form of solicitar. It presents a formal request or application as an ongoing action.

example.en: I am applying for a scholarship.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: A departamento can be a division within an organization. In some countries it can also mean an apartment or an administrative region.

example.es: Envía el formulario al departamento correcto.
example.en: Send the form to the correct department.

cards.noteEn: Fecha is the calendar date associated with an event or document.

example.es: Escribe la fecha en la primera línea.
example.en: Write the date on the first line.

cards.noteEn: Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Tuviste is the informal singular completed-past form of tener. It refers to something one person had at a finished time.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Prueba can mean a test, but it also means information or material that supports a claim.

example.es: Necesitamos una prueba de que ocurrió.
example.en: We need proof that it happened.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the statement that some evidence supports?
cards.answerEn: Use prueba de que, followed by the statement.
cards.noteEn: Prueba names the evidence, de links it to its content, and que introduces a complete idea with its own verb.

example.es: Esta foto es prueba de que llegaron temprano.
example.en: This photo is proof that they arrived early.

cards.answerEn: of; introducing what the evidence proves
cards.noteEn: After prueba, de can introduce the content supported by the evidence. When a whole statement follows, Spanish uses de que.

example.es: Hay pruebas de que el plan funciona.
example.en: There is evidence that the plan works.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: to them/anyone; replaces le before lo
cards.noteEn: When le or les comes immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it changes to se. This se identifies the recipient; it is not reflexive.

example.es: Le doy el libro a Ana. → Se lo doy.
example.en: I give the book to Ana. → I give it to her.

cards.promptEs: le/les + lo/la/los/las → se lo/se la/se los/se las
cards.answerEn: Use se for the recipient, followed by lo, la, los, or las for the thing.
cards.noteEn: Le or les normally means “to him,” “to her,” “to you” (formal), or “to them.” Immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it changes to se; Spanish does not say le lo. Se still stands for the recipient, while the second word stands for the thing. Le doy el libro a Ana therefore becomes se lo doy.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “I give it to her/him/them” without repeating the person and the thing?

example.es: Le doy el libro a Ana. → Se lo doy.
example.en: I give the book to Ana. → I give it to her.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.noteEn: Dije is the completed-past form of decir for the speaker.
Amigo can identify a male friend or appear as the masculine dictionary form when discussing the word itself.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
Preguntarle combines preguntar with attached le. The unchanged dictionary form names the action, while le identifies one person being asked.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.
Estaba is a background-past form of estar. The subject can be I, he, she, or one formal you; here the unstated subject is the speaker.

example.en: I was tired after the trip.

cards.promptEs: estar en plan + actitud o palabras aproximadas
cards.questionEn: How can colloquial Spanish frame someone's attitude, manner, or loose quotation?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of estar followed by en plan, then give the attitude or approximate words.
cards.noteEn: This informal expression is especially common in Spain. It can describe a mood or work much like conversational English 'be like' before an approximate quotation.

example.en: We were in a relaxed sort of mood.

cards.answerEn: in (fixed part of estar en plan)
cards.noteEn: En belongs to the colloquial expression estar en plan. The expression presents someone's attitude, mode, or approximate words.

example.en: She was in an optimistic sort of mood.

cards.answerEn: mode; like (fixed part of estar en plan)
cards.noteEn: In colloquial estar en plan, plan does not mean a literal plan. It helps frame an attitude, manner, or loose quotation.

example.en: He was like, 'It's no big deal.'

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.
Sería is the “would” form of ser, “to be.” Spanish keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds -ía.

example.en: It would be a good solution.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.
Buena has the feminine ending because it describes the feminine noun idea.

cards.questionEn: Where do common judgment words such as bueno or malo often go?
cards.answerEn: Put them before the noun when they give an overall evaluation: buena idea, mala noticia.
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts a neutral descriptive word after its noun, but common evaluation words can come before it. The describing word still changes to match the noun: bueno becomes buena before a feminine singular noun.
In plan de negocio, de negocio classifies the plan as a business plan.

example.es: Prepararon un plan de negocio sencillo.
example.en: They prepared a simple business plan.

cards.noteEn: The written accent distinguishes the pronoun él from the article el, which means “the.”
Respondió is the third-person singular completed-past form of responder.
In business and economics, beneficios commonly means the money left as profit, not merely general advantages.

example.es: La compañía declaró beneficios este año.
example.en: The company reported profits this year.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone deserves something, using the common pattern with me, te, se, nos, or os?
cards.answerEn: Put the matching small pronoun before a form of merecer that matches the person and time, then name the deserved thing.
cards.noteEn: For example, te mereces is used with tú and se merece with él, ella, or usted. The thing deserved can follow the verb or be understood from context.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: you; for yourself (small pronoun used with merecerse)
cards.noteEn: With informal singular tú, te is the matching small pronoun in merecerse algo. It appears before a form that matches the person and time, such as mereces.
Mereces is the informal singular present form of merecer. In the common pronominal pattern, it appears as te mereces.
Sé is the irregular affirmative command of ser for one familiar listener. Its written accent distinguishes it from se.
Justo describes a masculine singular person, choice, or result that is fair or morally right.

example.en: We are seeking a fair agreement.

cards.noteEn: Dirección can mean direction, management, or an address. With postal, it is the address used for mail.

example.es: Confirma tu dirección antes del envío.

cards.questionEn: How do you say mailing address or postal address?
cards.noteEn: Postal follows the feminine noun dirección but has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.es: La solicitud pide una dirección postal.
example.en: The application asks for a mailing address.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.
After a noun, postal describes something belonging to or used by the mail service, such as una balanza postal or un código postal.
